HVAC Services in Houston, TX: What Each One Covers

Repair, replacement, heating, maintenance and commercial systems, each explained in plain words. Find the one that fits your problem, then call the free line any hour to reach an independent, locally owned HVAC company.

Call (832) 662-4107 Match your problem to a page
  1. Home
  2. Services

A call goes faster when you can name the problem in a sentence. This page gathers every HVAC service in Houston, TX that the line takes calls about, with what each one covers and a link to its full page.

Houston Air & Heating never visits your home. Phone (832) 662-4107, let the automated assistant know if it is a heating or a cooling problem, which part of the area you are in and what you are seeing, and it hands your call to a locally owned, independent company that does the work. Those companies handle HVAC repair services in Houston, TX and the suburbs around it, and they set their own prices. Use the descriptions below to pick the right words, or skip straight to the table that matches symptoms to pages.

Cooling services

In a city where summer afternoons sit in the mid 90s for weeks, cooling problems are the most urgent ones. Cooling work splits into four kinds of visit.

AC repair

A system that blows warm, short cycles (turns on and off every few minutes), freezes up or will not start. A careful technician tests before replacing anything: electrical readings on the capacitor and contactor, refrigerant pressures, airflow and the condensate drain. See AC repair in Houston.

Air conditioning repair, part by part

If you want to understand the parts that wear out in Gulf Coast humidity, from coils to blower motors, and how each repair is done, the air conditioning repair page covers them one at a time.

Emergency and after-hours AC repair

For a house that is heating up overnight, an older relative or a baby at home, or a system that quit after a storm knocked out power. The line answers at any hour; what the company charges for a night or weekend visit is up to the company, so ask. See emergency AC repair.

AC installation and replacement

A new system should be sized by a load calculation of your house, not by the size of the old unit. A complete quote names the equipment model numbers, the efficiency rating, what happens to the ductwork and who pulls the permit. Inside Houston city limits, the Houston Permitting Center requires a mechanical permit for installing or replacing a condensing unit, followed by a city inspection. See AC installation in Houston.

Heating services

Houston homes heat in two main ways: a gas furnace, usually in the attic or a closet, or electric heat, either a heat pump or resistance heat strips in the air handler. They fail differently, so they have separate pages.

Furnace repair

A gas furnace that clicks but will not light, lights and shuts off, or fills the house with a burning smell on its first run of the season. Burners, gas valves and flue venting are technician work only. See furnace repair in Houston.

Heating repair: heat pumps and electric heat

A heat pump that blows cool air in heat mode, runs on emergency or auxiliary heat all night, or ices over and never defrosts. See heating repair.

Smell gas? Leave the house without flipping switches, then call 911 and the gas utility's leak line from a safe distance. If a carbon monoxide alarm sounds, get everyone outside and call 911.

Maintenance and commercial systems

HVAC tune-up and maintenance

A spring cooling check and a fall heating check catch weak parts, dirty coils and slow drains before they turn into a breakdown. The tune-up page explains how often to book one, and is a tune-up worth it weighs the evidence.

Commercial HVAC

Rooftop package units, split systems in offices and shops, and the cooling a restaurant kitchen needs. Commercial work is a different scale, and Texas license classes reflect it. See commercial HVAC in Houston.

What the line does not take calls about

The same phone number also handles Houston roofing and pressure washing calls, which is why the assistant asks what you need first. On this site, though, the subject is heating and cooling only. These jobs belong to other trades:

  • Plumbing, including water heaters, drains and gas piping to appliances. The water heater guide explains who to call.
  • Electrical work beyond the HVAC equipment itself, such as panel upgrades or new circuits.
  • Duct cleaning sold as a separate service. Duct repair and sealing that is part of an HVAC job is a question for the HVAC company.
  • Roofing and pressure washing are not covered on this site.
  • Appliance repair: refrigerators, washers, dryers and ovens.

Before you approve any work

The companies you reach are independent businesses. You decide whether to hire them, and you are free to get a second quote. Ask for the diagnosis in plain words, the price in writing and the company's Texas license number.

Verify the license before work begins. Texas requires anyone contracting to do air conditioning, refrigeration or heating work to hold an Air Conditioning and Refrigeration (ACR) Contractor license from the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR). Ask the company for its ACR license number, then confirm it on the TDLR license search (opens in a new tab). The line does not check this for you.

  1. Dial the numberAn automated assistant picks up (832) 662-4107 at any hour and asks what you need help with.
  2. Say what is wrongTell it whether the trouble is cooling or heating, where in the Houston area you are, and what the system is doing.
  3. Reach a local companyYour call is transferred to an independent, locally owned HVAC company, which gets a short summary of your problem before it answers.
  4. Work it out with themThat company inspects, quotes, repairs and bills you directly. If nobody can pick up, your name, number and problem are passed on for a call back.

Common questions

What HVAC services can I get through the Houston line?

Air conditioning repair, after-hours and emergency cooling calls, new system installation and replacement, gas furnace repair, heat pump and electric heat repair, seasonal tune-ups, and commercial rooftop and office systems. The line itself does none of this work. It transfers your call to an independent company that does.

Is an HVAC tune-up the same thing as a repair?

No. A tune-up is planned upkeep on a system that still runs: cleaning, measuring and checking parts before they wear out. A repair deals with a fault that is already there: a part that failed or a system that runs poorly. If the house is warm and the AC is blowing room temperature air, ask for a repair visit. The tune-up checklist shows what a full maintenance visit covers.

Does Houston require a permit for a new air conditioner?

Inside the City of Houston, yes. The Houston Permitting Center requires a mechanical permit for installing, repairing or replacing condensing units, and the work must pass a city inspection. Suburbs set their own rules. The licensed contractor normally pulls the permit, so ask about it when you get a replacement quote.

Can a Houston business call the line about a rooftop unit?

Yes. Offices, shops, restaurants and warehouses go through the same way: the assistant asks what is going on and transfers the call to an independent company that takes commercial work. See commercial HVAC.

Does the line handle plumbing, duct cleaning or appliance repair?

No. This site covers heating and air conditioning only. Water heaters, drains and pipes are plumbing work, and duct cleaning sold on its own, electrical panel work and appliance repair go to those trades. The water heater guide explains who to call for that.
